title: Database Reliability Engineering
blurb: Keeping data safe, fast and available, built up from first principles.

topics.title: Durability & the Write-Ahead Log
topics.one_liner: How a database promises that a committed write survives a power cut, using one append-only file.

first_principles.problem:
A program keeps data in memory because memory is fast. Memory is also volatile: pull the plug and every byte is gone. Disks keep data, but they are thousands of times slower, and writing a page in the middle of a big file means a random seek.

So a database is stuck between two bad options. Write every change straight to its final place on disk and it is slow. Keep changes in memory and flush later, and a crash loses them, possibly leaving half-written pages behind.
truths: Memory (RAM) loses everything on power loss; only storage (disk/SSD) survives.
Sequential writes (appending to the end of a file) are far cheaper than random writes scattered across a file.
A write isn't really on disk until the OS is told to flush it (`fsync`). Before that it may only be in a cache.
A crash can happen between *any* two instructions, including halfway through writing a page.
derivation: We can't afford a random write to every data page on each commit, so keep the **data pages in memory** (the buffer pool) and change them there.
We still need the change to survive a crash, so before saying "committed", **append a small record describing the change** to a separate log file. Appending is sequential, so it's cheap.
**`fsync` the log** at commit. Now the change is on durable storage, even though the data page itself is still only in memory.
Data pages get written to disk **later, in the background, in batches** (checkpoints). That's the expensive work, but it's off the critical path.
After a crash, start from the last checkpoint and **replay the log** to redo anything that hadn't reached the data files yet. Log first, data later: that's the *write-ahead* rule.

analogy.title: The restaurant order pad
analogy.story:
A busy kitchen doesn't rearrange the pantry every time an order comes in. The waiter writes each order on a numbered pad in the order it arrives. That takes seconds. The cooks work through the orders and the pantry stock gets updated later.

If the head chef faints mid-service, nobody panics. The replacement reads the pad from the last "stock-take" line onwards and knows exactly which orders were promised. Nothing a customer was told "yes, it's coming" about is lost, because the promise was written down *before* it was made.
analogy.breaks: A real pad never gets corrupted halfway through a line. A disk write can, so real WALs add checksums to every record and torn records at the end are discarded on recovery.

branches.label: Checkpoints
children: Allow old WAL to be recycled

example.title: An UPDATE that survives a power cut
example.scenario: A user changes their email. The app runs `UPDATE users SET email='new@x.com' WHERE id=42;` and gets a success. One second later the server loses power, before the table's data page was ever written to disk.

steps.label: In memory
steps.detail: Postgres loads the page holding row 42 into shared buffers and changes it there. The page is now *dirty*: newer than the on-disk copy.

steps.label: Logged
steps.detail: A WAL record saying "in page X, row 42 now has email new@x.com" is appended to `pg_wal/`, tagged with a log sequence number (LSN).

steps.label: Durable
steps.detail: On `COMMIT`, Postgres fsyncs the WAL up to that LSN. Only then does the client get success.

steps.label: Crash
steps.detail: Power dies. The dirty page in memory is lost. The data file still has the old email.

steps.label: Recovery
steps.detail: On boot, Postgres finds the last checkpoint and replays every WAL record after it. Row 42 gets its new email back before any client can connect.

example.outcome: the client was told "done", the machine crashed, and after restart the data is exactly as promised. The only cost was one small sequential write per commit.

summary.core: Write down what you are about to change in an append-only log, flush that log, and only then say "committed". The real data can catch up later because the log can always rebuild it.
points: **Commit = WAL flushed**, not data file written.
Checkpoints trade write bursts for shorter crash recovery.
The same log powers **replication, backups (PITR) and CDC**. Learn the WAL once and it explains half of DBRE.
Turning off `fsync` makes benchmarks fast and makes data corruption after a crash possible. Never do it in production.

check.q: Why is appending to the WAL cheaper than writing the table page directly?
check.a: Appends are sequential and small. Updating table pages means random writes of whole pages (8 KB in Postgres) scattered across many files.

check.q: What happens to recovery time if checkpoints are very far apart?
check.a: More WAL piles up after the last checkpoint, so recovery has more to replay and takes longer. More frequent checkpoints shorten recovery but cause more write I/O.

topics.title: ACID Transactions
topics.one_liner: Four promises that let many users change shared data without ever seeing half-finished work.

first_principles.problem:
Real business actions are made of several writes. Moving $100 means one balance goes down and another goes up. If the program crashes between the two, money disappears. If two people run it at the same time, they can overwrite each other.

Without help from the database, every application would have to solve crash safety and concurrency itself, and most would get it wrong.
truths: A process can crash between any two statements.
Many clients act on the same rows at the same time.
Some rules ("balance >= 0", "order must reference a real customer") must always hold.
Once you tell a user "done", they act on it, so you can't take it back.
derivation: Group the writes of one action into a unit and promise **all or nothing**: Atomicity. On failure, undo the partial work.
Check the declared rules at the unit's end and refuse to commit if any would break: **Consistency** (constraints, foreign keys, checks).
Make concurrent units behave *as if* they ran one at a time, at least to a chosen degree: **Isolation**.
Once committed, survive crashes: **Durability**, provided by the WAL from the previous concept.
Give the programmer two words for all of this: `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` (or `ROLLBACK`).

analogy.title: A bank teller's sealed envelope
analogy.story:
You hand a teller a slip: "take $100 from savings, put it in checking". The teller does both steps behind the counter, out of view, then stamps the slip. Until the stamp, nobody else in the bank sees anything change. If the alarm goes off mid-task, the teller tears up the slip and both accounts look untouched.

The stamp is final. Even if the branch burns down, the head office ledger already has it.
mapping: Work done out of view until stamped
analogy.breaks: A teller works one customer at a time. A database runs thousands of transactions *truly* in parallel and only *pretends* they're isolated, and how well it pretends depends on the isolation level (next concept).

example.title: Transferring money, with a crash in the middle
example.scenario: Alice sends Bob $100. The app server is killed after the first UPDATE runs but before COMMIT.

steps.label: Begin
steps.detail: The transaction starts. Changes are visible only to this transaction.

steps.label: Debit
steps.detail: Alice's row is updated to `balance - 100`. Other sessions still see her old balance.

steps.label: Crash
steps.detail: The app dies. Postgres notices the closed connection and aborts the open transaction.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: The debit is never visible to anyone. Run it again and it works, because no half-transfer was left behind.

example.outcome: money never vanishes and never appears out of nowhere. Any failure before COMMIT leaves the world exactly as it was.

summary.core: A transaction lets you treat several writes as one indivisible, rule-checked, crash-proof step, so concurrency and crashes stop being your application's problem.
points: **A** = all-or-nothing, **C** = rules hold, **I** = no peeking at half-done work, **D** = committed means kept.
The "C" only covers rules you *declare*. Put invariants in constraints.
Long transactions hold locks and block cleanup (vacuum). Keep them short and never wait on the network inside one.

check.q: Is a CHECK constraint part of Atomicity or Consistency?
check.a: Consistency. It's a rule the database enforces before allowing commit. Atomicity is about the transaction's writes landing together or not at all.

check.q: Why is calling a payment API inside a transaction dangerous?
check.a: The transaction stays open (holding locks) while you wait on the network, and if the DB later rolls back, the external charge can't be undone with it.

topics.title: Isolation Levels & MVCC
topics.one_liner: How readers and writers share the same rows without blocking each other, and which anomalies each level still allows.

first_principles.problem:
Perfect isolation means every transaction runs as if it were alone. The simple way to get that is to lock everything a transaction touches, but then readers wait for writers, writers wait for readers, and throughput collapses.

We want high concurrency *and* sane results. Those goals conflict, so databases offer a menu of compromises.
truths: A read that sees half of another transaction's work gives wrong answers.
Locking a row makes everyone else who needs it wait.
Most workloads are read-heavy, so readers blocking writers (or the reverse) is very costly.
Storage is cheap compared with waiting.
derivation: Instead of overwriting a row, **write a new version** of it and keep the old one around for a while.
Stamp each version with the transaction that created it (and the one that deleted it).
Give each transaction a **snapshot**: the set of transactions committed when it started (or when each statement started).
A reader picks the version visible in its snapshot, so **readers never block writers and writers never block readers**. This is MVCC.
Old versions nobody can see any more are **garbage-collected** later (Postgres: `VACUUM`).
Choose how fresh the snapshot is and how strictly conflicts are checked: that choice is the **isolation level**.

analogy.title: A shared document with version history
analogy.story:
Imagine a team document where nobody edits in place. Every edit creates a new revision. When you open the document, you are pinned to the revision that was current when you opened it, so you read a stable copy even while colleagues keep editing.

When you save, the system checks whether someone else changed the same paragraph since your revision. Depending on how strict the team is, it either lets you overwrite them, warns you, or rejects your save and asks you to redo it on top of the latest version.
mapping: How strict the save check is
analogy.breaks: Document tools merge paragraph by paragraph. Databases also have to catch conflicts on rows that *didn't exist yet* (phantoms) and on decisions made from aggregates, which is what `SERIALIZABLE` adds.

example.title: Two doctors and the on-call rule (write skew)
example.scenario: Rule: at least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call. Each opens the app at the same moment, sees "2 on call", and signs off. Each transaction checked the rule and passed, yet together they broke it.

steps.label: READ COMMITTED / REPEATABLE READ
steps.detail: Both commits succeed. They updated *different rows*, so there's no row conflict to detect. This is **write skew**.

steps.label: SERIALIZABLE
steps.detail: Postgres tracks that each transaction read data the other one changed. The second commit fails with `could not serialize access`.

steps.label: App retries
steps.detail: The retried transaction now sees "1 on call", and the app refuses Bob's sign-off. The rule holds.

example.outcome: under weaker levels the rule silently breaks. Under SERIALIZABLE (or with explicit row locks) one doctor gets an error and a retry gives the right answer.

summary.core: MVCC gives each transaction its own consistent snapshot by keeping old row versions, and the isolation level decides how many concurrency anomalies you're willing to tolerate in exchange for speed.
points: Postgres default is **READ COMMITTED**: each *statement* sees fresh committed data, so two reads in one transaction can differ.
**Write skew** survives REPEATABLE READ. Use SERIALIZABLE or `FOR UPDATE` for check-then-act rules.
Using SERIALIZABLE means your app **must retry** on 40001.
MVCC's bill is dead tuples. A long-running transaction stops VACUUM and tables bloat.

check.q: Why do readers not block writers under MVCC?
check.a: The writer creates a new row version. The reader keeps reading the older version that its snapshot can see, so neither waits on the other.

check.q: Why can an idle-in-transaction session cause table bloat?
check.a: Its snapshot is still open, so VACUUM can't remove row versions that snapshot might need. Dead tuples pile up across the whole database.

topics.title: Indexes & Query Plans
topics.one_liner: Why one missing index turns a 2 ms query into a 20 s one, and how the planner decides what to do.

first_principles.problem:
A table is a pile of pages. To find `WHERE email = 'x'` with nothing else to go on, the database must read every page and check every row. That's fine for 1,000 rows and terrible for 100 million.

We need a way to jump straight to the matching rows. We also need something to decide, for every query, which of several ways to get the data is cheapest.
truths: Reading a page from disk costs far more than comparing values in memory.
Sorted data can be searched by halving (binary search): log₂(100 million) ≈ 27 steps.
Every extra copy of data must be updated on every write.
The best strategy depends on how many rows match, which is data-dependent.
derivation: Keep a **separate sorted structure** of (key → row location) for the columns you search by.
Make it a wide, shallow tree (**B-tree**) so that finding any key takes only 3–4 page reads, even for huge tables.
Because it's sorted, the same index also answers ranges (`>`, `BETWEEN`) and `ORDER BY` without a sort step.
Accept the cost: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update every index, so **don't index everything**.
Let a **planner** estimate each strategy's cost from table statistics (row counts, value distribution) and pick the cheapest. Sometimes that is a full scan.

analogy.title: The index at the back of a textbook
analogy.story:
To find every page that mentions "photosynthesis", you could read the whole 900-page book, or flip to the alphabetical index at the back, find the word in seconds, and jump to pages 112 and 340.

But if you want every page that mentions "the", the index is useless. You'd be flipping back and forth for every page, and it's faster to just read the book cover to cover. A good reader, like a good query planner, knows which approach to use.
mapping: Page numbers next to each word
analogy.breaks: A book index never goes stale. A database's *statistics* can, so the planner may make bad choices until `ANALYZE` refreshes them.

example.title: Fixing a slow "recent orders" page
example.scenario: The "My orders" page loads in 4 seconds. The table has 50 million orders, and the query is `WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`.

steps.label: Measure
steps.detail: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows a **Seq Scan** that reads 50 M rows and keeps 312, followed by a **Sort**.

steps.label: Reason
steps.detail: There's an index on `created_at` only. To use it, the database would walk all orders newest first and filter by customer, which is too slow, so it scans the table instead.

steps.label: Design
steps.detail: Put the equality column first, then the sort column: `(customer_id, created_at DESC)`. The index now holds each customer's orders already in the order the page needs.

steps.label: Build safely
steps.detail: Use `CONCURRENTLY` so production writes aren't blocked while the index builds.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: The new plan is an **Index Scan** that stops after 20 rows. No sort, a handful of page reads.

example.outcome: the same query reads about 5 pages instead of about 600,000. Writes to `orders` pay a small extra cost to maintain one more index.

summary.core: An index is a sorted shortcut to rows that trades write cost and space for read speed, and the planner uses statistics to decide whether the shortcut is worth taking for each query.
points: Always read the **actual** plan (`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) before adding an index.
Composite index column order: **equality → range/sort**.
A seq scan isn't always bad. For queries matching most of the table it's the fastest option.
Drop unused indexes. They slow every write and help nothing.

check.q: Would an index on (created_at, customer_id) help the example query as well?
check.a: Much less. The leading column is created_at, so the customer's rows are scattered throughout the index. Equality columns should come first.

check.q: Why might the planner ignore a perfectly good index?
check.a: Its row estimate says many rows match (so a scan is cheaper), or the statistics are stale. Run ANALYZE and compare estimated with actual rows.

topics.title: Replication
topics.one_liner: Keeping copies of the database on other machines by shipping the change log, and the lag that comes with it.

first_principles.problem:
One database server is a single point of failure. If its disk dies, data is gone, and if the machine is down, the app is down. One server also has a ceiling on how many reads it can serve.

We need several machines holding the same data. But copying a live, constantly changing database between machines is hard, and the network between them is slow and unreliable.
truths: Any single machine, disk or data centre will eventually fail.
Network round-trips take time (≈0.5 ms in a zone, 10–80 ms across regions).
The primary already records every change, in order, in its WAL.
You can't wait for a remote ack *and* be as fast as not waiting.
derivation: Don't copy tables. **Stream the WAL** to other servers and have them replay it. The log already describes every change in order.
Replicas replay in the same order, so they end up in the **same state**, just slightly later.

Decide when the primary may say "committed": after its own disk flush (**asynchronous**: fast, but may lose the last few transactions on failover) or after a replica confirms (**synchronous**: no loss, but every commit pays a network round-trip).
Replicas can serve **read-only queries**, which spreads read load, but those reads may be slightly stale (**replication lag**).

analogy.title: The newsroom and its mirror offices
analogy.story:
The head office writes the newspaper and dictates every edit, in order, over the phone to branch offices that keep identical copies. Branches can hand out copies to local readers, so the head office isn't swamped.

Usually a branch is a few seconds behind. If the head office insists on hearing "got it" from a branch before announcing each edit, nothing can ever be lost, but every announcement waits for the phone call.
mapping: Branch being a few seconds behind
analogy.breaks: Branches can't reject an edit, but replicas *can* conflict with long-running read queries on them. Postgres will cancel such a query, or delay replay, depending on `max_standby_streaming_delay`.

example.title: "I just changed my name but the page shows the old one"
example.scenario: The app writes to the primary and reads from an async replica. A user updates their profile and is redirected to the profile page, which still shows the old name.

steps.label: Write
steps.detail: The name change commits on the primary at LSN `0/5A3F2C8`.

steps.label: Read
steps.detail: 80 ms later the read goes to a replica that has only replayed up to `0/5A3E000`, because a big batch job is saturating its disk.

steps.label: Diagnose
steps.detail: `pg_stat_replication` on the primary shows `replay_lag` of 300 ms on that replica.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Route a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write (**read-your-writes**), or wait until the replica has replayed past the write's LSN.

code.text:
-- On the primary: how far behind is each replica?
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS bytes_behind,
       replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- On a replica:
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS seconds_behind;

example.outcome: the data was never wrong, only late. Lag is a normal part of async replication, and the application has to be designed with it in mind.

summary.core: Replication copies the primary's ordered change log to other servers so they converge on the same data. Async is fast but can lose the last few commits and serve stale reads. Sync loses nothing but makes every commit slower.
points: Replication protects against **machine loss**, not **mistakes**. A `DROP TABLE` replicates instantly. You still need backups.
Always **monitor lag** in both bytes and seconds, and alert on it.
Reads from replicas need a read-your-writes strategy.
An abandoned replication slot keeps WAL forever and can fill the primary's disk.

check.q: With async replication and a failover, what data can be lost?
check.a: Transactions that committed on the primary but hadn't yet reached the replica that gets promoted. Roughly, the replication lag at the moment of failure.

check.q: Why isn't a replica a backup?
check.a: It faithfully copies every change, including accidental deletes and corruption caused by bad application writes. Backups let you go back in time; replicas only go forward.

topics.title: Failover & High Availability
topics.one_liner: Promoting a replica when the primary dies, without ending up with two primaries.

first_principles.problem:
Having a replica doesn't help much if, at 3 a.m., someone has to wake up, decide the primary is really dead, promote the replica by hand and repoint every application. That takes 30+ minutes of downtime.

Automating it is harder than it looks. A machine that *seems* dead may just be unreachable, and if you promote a new primary while the old one is still accepting writes, you get two diverging copies of the truth.
truths: From the outside you can't tell "crashed" apart from "network to it is broken".
Two nodes accepting writes for the same data will diverge, and merging them later is painful or impossible.
A majority of an odd-sized group can only exist on one side of a network split.
Detection, promotion and client re-routing each take time.
derivation: Run **several monitors** (or a consensus store such as etcd/Consul) rather than one, so a single observer's bad network can't trigger a failover.
Only fail over when a **majority (quorum)** agrees the primary is gone. A minority partition can't promote anyone.
Before or during promotion, **fence** the old primary: make sure it can't accept writes (revoke its leader lock, shut it down, cut its storage or IP).
Promote the **most up-to-date replica** (highest replayed LSN) to minimise data loss.
Point clients at a **stable endpoint** (DNS, virtual IP, proxy) that follows the leader, so apps don't need config changes.

analogy.title: Choosing a new captain on a ship
analogy.story:
If the captain stops answering the radio, the crew can't let any single sailor declare himself captain. The radio might just be broken. Instead, the officers vote, and a new captain is appointed only if a majority agrees.

The new captain's first order is to take the old captain's keys to the bridge. Even if the old captain walks back in, he can no longer steer the ship. Then the crew tells everyone "orders now come from the new bridge".
mapping: "Orders now come from the new bridge"
analogy.breaks: A ship's crew can see the captain. Database nodes only see packets, so heartbeat timeouts must be tuned. Too short and you get false failovers, too long and every real failure means more downtime.

example.title: A network split with Patroni + etcd
example.scenario: Three nodes: `db1` (primary) in zone A, `db2` and `db3` in zones B and C. Zone A's network partitions from the rest for 2 minutes.

steps.label: Lease expires
steps.detail: db1 holds the leader key in etcd with a 30 s TTL. Cut off from the etcd majority, it can't renew it.

steps.label: Self-fencing
steps.detail: Patroni on db1 sees it lost the lease and **demotes db1 to read-only**. It refuses writes even though the machine is healthy.

steps.label: Election
steps.detail: db2 and db3 (with the etcd majority) compare replay LSNs. db2 is further ahead and takes the leader key.

steps.label: Promotion
steps.detail: db2 is promoted. HAProxy's health check (`/primary` returns 200 only on the leader) starts sending writes to db2.

steps.label: Healing
steps.detail: When zone A returns, db1 uses `pg_rewind` to discard any unreplicated divergence and rejoins as a replica of db2.

code.text:
# patroni.yml (excerpt)
bootstrap:
  dcs:
    ttl: 30                     # leader lease
    loop_wait: 10
    retry_timeout: 10
    maximum_lag_on_failover: 1048576   # don't promote a replica >1 MB behind
    postgresql:
      use_pg_rewind: true

example.outcome: about 30–45 seconds of write unavailability, never two primaries, and at most the async lag lost. Nobody was paged to make the decision.

summary.core: Safe failover is a majority vote plus fencing. Only a quorum can name a new primary, and the old one must be stopped from writing before or as the new one starts.
points: Split-brain is worse than downtime. **Fencing is not optional.**
Use an odd number of voters (3 or 5) across failure domains.
Failover only helps if clients **reconnect and retry**. Test that path.
Practise it: scheduled failover drills turn a scary event into a routine one.

check.q: Why do you need 3 etcd nodes rather than 2?
check.a: With 2, a split leaves 1 vs 1 and neither side has a majority, so no one can decide. With 3, one side always has 2 of 3.

check.q: What is split-brain and why is it so bad?
check.a: Two nodes both believe they're primary and accept writes. The data diverges and there's no automatic way to merge the two histories.

topics.title: Backups, PITR, RPO & RTO
topics.one_liner: Being able to rewind the database to just before the mistake, and knowing how long that takes.

first_principles.problem:
Replication protects against hardware failure, but it faithfully copies human mistakes too. A bad migration, a `DELETE` without `WHERE`, or ransomware all land on every replica within milliseconds.

We need copies frozen in the past, and the ability to restore to any moment, not just to last night.
truths: The most likely cause of data loss is a person or a bug, not a disk.
A full copy of a large database is slow and expensive to take often.
The WAL already contains every change since a given point, in order.
A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup.
derivation: Take a **base backup** (a full physical copy) periodically, say daily.
**Archive every WAL segment** continuously to separate storage (e.g. S3).
To restore to any moment T: restore the base backup taken before T, then **replay archived WAL up to T**. That's **point-in-time recovery (PITR)**.
Define targets: **RPO**, how much data you can afford to lose (set by WAL archiving frequency), and **RTO**, how long recovery may take (set by base-backup age, replay speed and restore bandwidth).
**Restore automatically on a schedule** and verify the result, so you know your real RTO before an incident tells you.

analogy.title: A video game's save points plus a replay recording
analogy.story:
A game saves your full progress every evening (a save point). It also records every move you make. If at 14:32 you walk off a cliff, you don't want last night's save, you want 14:31.

So you load last night's save and fast-forward the recording to 14:31, then stop. The older the save point, the longer the fast-forward takes.
mapping: Moves not yet recorded when it crashed
analogy.breaks: A game recording is tiny. WAL for a busy database can be hundreds of GB per day, so restore bandwidth and replay speed dominate RTO. Take base backups more often to keep replay short.

example.title: Rewinding an accidental DELETE
example.scenario: At 14:32:10 a developer runs `DELETE FROM invoices;` on production (meant for staging). The deletion replicates everywhere within seconds. Last base backup: 02:00. WAL is archived to S3 every minute.

steps.label: Find the moment
steps.detail: From logs / `pg_stat_statements`, the bad statement ran at **14:32:10**. Target: `14:32:09`.

steps.label: Restore beside, not over
steps.detail: Spin up a **new** server and restore the 02:00 base backup there. Production keeps running so new invoices aren't lost.

steps.label: Replay
steps.detail: Recovery replays about 12 h of archived WAL and stops at the target time. (Replay speed is what sets the RTO here.)

steps.label: Recover the rows
steps.detail: Copy the `invoices` table from the restored server back into production (e.g. `pg_dump -t invoices` → load into a temp table → insert the missing rows).

code.text:
# postgresql.conf on the restore server (Postgres 12+; also create recovery.signal)
restore_command        = 'wal-g wal-fetch %f %p'
recovery_target_time   = '2026-10-11 14:32:09+00'
recovery_target_action = 'pause'      # look around before promoting

wal-g backup-fetch /var/lib/postgresql/data LATEST   # base backup before the target
touch /var/lib/postgresql/data/recovery.signal && pg_ctl start

example.outcome: every invoice that existed one second before the mistake is back, and nothing written to production after the mistake was lost. RPO ≈ 0 for this kind of failure, RTO ≈ restore time plus replay time.

summary.core: Base backups plus a continuous WAL archive let you rebuild the database at any second in the past. RPO and RTO turn "we have backups" into a promise you can measure.
points: Replicas guard against hardware loss. **Backups guard against mistakes.** You need both.
Restore to a **separate** server, then copy back what you need.
Untested backups don't count. **Automate restore drills** and record the real RTO.
Keep backups where the same credentials that can delete prod **can't delete them**.

check.q: Your base backups are weekly and WAL replay runs at 1 hour of WAL per 10 minutes. Worst-case replay time?
check.a: Up to 7 days of WAL → about 70 × 10 min ≈ 11.7 hours of replay alone. More frequent base backups cut RTO.

check.q: Which number does WAL archiving frequency mostly control: RPO or RTO?
check.a: RPO. It decides how much recent history might not yet be safe off-site when disaster strikes.

topics.title: Connection Pooling
topics.one_liner: Why 5,000 app connections can kill a database that 50 connections would run happily.

first_principles.problem:
Every Postgres connection is a full operating-system process with its own memory. Opening one costs a fork and an authentication handshake, often several milliseconds.

Modern apps autoscale to hundreds of pods, each opening dozens of connections, so the database ends up spending its CPU and memory managing thousands of mostly idle connections instead of running queries.
truths: A database can only run as many queries truly in parallel as it has CPU cores (plus some I/O wait).
Each connection consumes memory (several MB in Postgres) even when idle.
Opening a connection is far slower than reusing one.
Most app connections are idle most of the time.
derivation: Since only about *cores × 2–4* queries can usefully run at once, extra connections only add **contention and memory pressure**.
So put a **pooler** between apps and the database. Apps open many cheap client connections to the pooler, and the pooler keeps a **small, fixed set of real server connections**.
Hand a real connection to a client only while it needs one: per **transaction** (most efficient) or per **session** (most compatible).
Queue the rest briefly instead of overloading the database, so **back-pressure** replaces collapse.

analogy.title: Checkout lanes at a supermarket
analogy.story: A supermarket with 8 tills doesn't hire one cashier per shopper. Shoppers browse (idle) most of the time and only need a cashier for a minute at checkout. A short queue in front of 8 busy tills moves faster than 500 people crowding around 500 half-asleep cashiers in a room built for 8.
analogy.breaks: Shoppers don't care which cashier they get. Some database features remember state *per connection* (session `SET`s, advisory locks, some prepared statements, `LISTEN`), and those can break when transaction pooling hands you a different connection each time.

example.title: An autoscaling event that took down the database
example.scenario: Black Friday: the API scales from 20 to 200 pods, each with a pool of 20 connections. The database (16 vCPU, max_connections=500) starts rejecting connections and latency explodes.

steps.label: Symptom
steps.detail: `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`. The connections that did get through slow down because hundreds of processes fight for 16 cores.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: At any instant only about 30–60 queries are actually running. The rest of the connections are idle.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Put PgBouncer in **transaction mode** in front. The apps keep their pools (now pointing at PgBouncer), and PgBouncer keeps `default_pool_size = 40` real connections.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: The database sees 40 busy connections. Bursts queue for a few ms in PgBouncer instead of overwhelming Postgres.

code.text:
; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
shop = host=10.0.1.5 dbname=shop

[pgbouncer]
pool_mode          = transaction
max_client_conn    = 5000     ; cheap: just sockets
default_pool_size  = 40       ; real Postgres connections
query_wait_timeout = 5        ; fail fast instead of queueing forever

example.outcome: the same traffic, served by about 10× fewer database connections, with lower latency and room left for spikes.

summary.core: A database does its best work with a small number of busy connections. A pooler turns thousands of mostly idle app connections into that small busy set and queues the overflow.
points: More connections ≠ more throughput. Past about cores × a few, it gets **worse**.
Transaction pooling gives the best ratio but breaks per-session state. Audit your use of `SET`, advisory locks and `LISTEN`.
Kill **idle-in-transaction** sessions (`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`). They hold a pooled slot and block vacuum.

check.q: Why can't you just raise max_connections to 5,000?
check.a: Each connection is a process with its own memory. Thousands of them exhaust RAM and cause CPU contention and lock-manager overhead, so throughput falls.

check.q: What breaks under transaction-mode pooling?
check.a: Anything that relies on the same server connection across transactions: session-level SET, advisory locks held across transactions, LISTEN/NOTIFY, temp tables, and older prepared-statement setups.

topics.title: Partitioning & Sharding
topics.one_liner: Splitting data so no single table or server has to hold, or serve, all of it.

first_principles.problem:
Tables and traffic grow, but a single server has hard limits: disk size, write throughput, memory for hot data. Even before those limits, giant tables make maintenance (vacuum, index rebuilds, deleting old data) painfully slow.

We need to split the data into pieces. The difficulty is splitting it so that most queries still only touch one piece.
truths: One machine has finite CPU, RAM, disk and write bandwidth.
Work on a smaller dataset is faster: smaller indexes fit in memory and vacuum finishes sooner.
A query that must ask every piece is as slow as the slowest piece.
Moving data between pieces later is expensive.
derivation: First split **within one server**: **partition** a big table by time or key, so old data is dropped as whole partitions and queries skip irrelevant ones (**partition pruning**).
When one server isn't enough, split **across servers**: **sharding**. Each shard owns a subset of keys.
Choose a **shard key** that most queries include (e.g. `tenant_id`), so a request goes to exactly one shard.
Spread keys evenly (**hash**) or by range. Watch for **hot keys** that overload one shard.
Accept the costs: cross-shard joins and transactions become hard, and rebalancing needs a plan from day one.

analogy.title: A library that outgrows its building
analogy.story:
At first, one library holds all the books. It gets crowded, so it organises them into rooms by year (partitions). You go straight to the 2026 room, and clearing out 1990s magazines means emptying one room.

Eventually the city builds branch libraries, each owning authors A–F, G–M and so on (shards). Finding one book is easy because you know which branch to go to. A request for "every book published in 2026, sorted by title" means visiting every branch and merging the lists.
mapping: Rooms by year in one building
One branch swamped by a bestseller
analogy.breaks: Moving books between branches is a weekend job. Moving live data between shards while it's being written requires careful dual-writes or logical replication.

example.title: Partitioning a 2-billion-row events table by month
example.scenario: `events` gets 30 M rows/day. Deleting rows older than 90 days takes hours, bloats the table and causes replication lag. Dashboards query the last 7 days.

steps.label: Create partitioned parent
steps.detail: `PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at)` with one child table per month.

steps.label: Queries get pruned
steps.detail: `WHERE created_at > now() - interval '7 days'` only scans the current (and maybe previous) month's partition.

steps.label: Retention becomes free
steps.detail: Instead of `DELETE … WHERE created_at < …` (hours, bloat), run `DROP TABLE events_2026_06` (milliseconds, no bloat).

steps.label: Sharding not needed yet
steps.detail: Write volume fits one server. Sharding would add cross-shard complexity for no gain, so **partition first, shard when forced**.

example.outcome: dashboard queries read about 7 days of data instead of 2 billion rows, and retention is a metadata operation instead of a multi-hour delete.

summary.core: Split data so most work touches only a small piece: partitions within one server for manageability and pruning, shards across servers when one machine truly can't keep up. Pick the split key from your access pattern.
points: **Partitioning** is cheap and solves retention and pruning. **Sharding** solves scale but makes joins, transactions and operations harder.
The shard key is close to permanent. Choose one that appears in nearly every query.
Exhaust indexes, replicas, caching and vertical scaling before sharding.

check.q: Why is DROP of a partition so much better than DELETE for retention?
check.a: DROP removes the whole file in one metadata operation. DELETE marks each row dead (MVCC), generates WAL for every row, causes bloat and needs VACUUM afterwards.

check.q: You shard a multi-tenant SaaS by user_id, but most queries are per tenant. Problem?
check.a: A tenant's data is spread over all shards, so tenant queries become scatter-gather. tenant_id would keep each tenant on one shard.

topics.title: Zero-Downtime Schema Migrations
topics.one_liner: Changing the shape of a live table while old and new code both run against it.

first_principles.problem:
Applications change, so the schema must change: new columns, renamed fields, new indexes. Some DDL needs an exclusive lock that blocks every read and write on the table while it runs, and on a 500 GB table that can take minutes.

Also, during a rolling deploy, **old and new versions of the app run at the same time**, so for a while the schema has to work for both.
truths: Many `ALTER TABLE` forms take an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock. While waiting for it, they also queue every query behind them.
Rewriting a large table takes time proportional to its size.
During a rolling deploy, version N and version N+1 run simultaneously.
A deploy you can't roll back is a bet.
derivation: Never make a change that old code can't tolerate. Split every breaking change into **backward-compatible steps**: *expand*, then *migrate*, then *contract*.
**Expand**: add the new column/table (nullable, no rewrite). Old code ignores it.
**Migrate**: deploy code that writes to both old and new, **backfill** existing rows in small batches, then switch reads to the new column.
**Contract**: once nothing reads the old column, drop it in a later release.
Guard each DDL with a short **`lock_timeout`** so it gives up quickly instead of queueing the whole app behind it, and use online variants (`CONCURRENTLY`, `NOT VALID`).

analogy.title: Replacing a bridge while traffic keeps flowing
analogy.story:
You can't close the only bridge into the city for a week. So you build the new bridge next to the old one, open it, and divert traffic lane by lane. Only when the last car has moved over do you demolish the old bridge.

At no point is there zero bridges, and if the new one has a problem, the old one is still standing.
analogy.breaks: Bridges don't have locks. The surprise in databases is that even a *fast* DDL waiting for a lock blocks everything queued behind it, which is why `lock_timeout` matters even for "instant" changes.

example.title: Renaming `users.name` to `users.full_name` on a busy table
example.scenario: A plain `ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name` would break every running pod still using `name` the instant it ran.

steps.label: Release 1: expand
steps.detail: `ADD COLUMN full_name text` (nullable, no default, so instant). Deploy code that writes **both** columns.

steps.label: Backfill
steps.detail: Copy `name` → `full_name` in chunks of about 5,000 rows, with pauses, so you don't create a huge transaction, lock storm or replication-lag spike.

steps.label: Release 2: switch
steps.detail: Code reads `full_name` and still writes both, so rolling back to release 1 is safe.

steps.label: Release 3: contract
steps.detail: Code stops touching `name`. In a later migration, `DROP COLUMN name`, guarded by `lock_timeout`.

example.outcome: three small releases instead of one risky one, every step reversible, and the table never locked for more than milliseconds.

summary.core: Never change the schema in a way that running code can't handle. Expand, migrate, then contract across separate releases, and make every DDL give up quickly rather than block the app.
points: Always `SET lock_timeout` before DDL on hot tables.
Use `CONCURRENTLY` for indexes and `NOT VALID` + `VALIDATE` for constraints.
Backfill in small batches and watch replication lag while you do it.
Renames and type changes are multi-release projects, not single migrations.

check.q: An ALTER that would take 2 ms caused a 40-second outage. How?
check.a: It waited for an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock behind a long-running query, and every new query on the table queued behind the waiting ALTER. lock_timeout would have made it give up and retry.

check.q: Why keep dual-writing during release 2?
check.a: So you can roll back to release 1 (which reads the old column) without losing data written in the meantime.

topics.title: Database SLOs & Observability
topics.one_liner: Knowing the database is healthy from the user's point of view, and finding why when it isn't.

first_principles.problem:
Databases expose hundreds of metrics. Teams either watch none of them and find out from customers, or alert on all of them and get paged at 3 a.m. for CPU at 81% while users are fine.

We need a small set of signals that reflect what users actually experience, plus enough detail to find the cause quickly.
truths: Users experience latency and errors, not CPU percentages.
Averages hide the slow requests. The slowest 1% is where users complain.
Most database slowness comes from a few query shapes.
Some failures build slowly (disk filling, bloat, wraparound) and give days of warning if you look.
derivation: Define **SLIs** from the client's view: query latency percentiles (p95/p99), error rate, and availability of a writeable primary.
Set **SLOs** on them (e.g. "99.9% of queries < 100 ms over 30 days") and **alert on error-budget burn**, not on raw resource metrics.
For diagnosis, group work by **query fingerprint** (`pg_stat_statements`) so you can see which shapes consume the time.
Watch **saturation**: connections, CPU, I/O wait, replication lag, locks.
Track **slow-building risks** as capacity trends: disk growth, bloat, transaction-ID age.

analogy.title: A car's dashboard versus the mechanic's diagnostic port
analogy.story:
The driver's dashboard shows a few things that matter: speed, fuel and a warning light. You don't want the oil-pressure graph on the dashboard. You want a light that turns on when something is actually wrong.

When it does, the mechanic plugs into the diagnostic port and reads hundreds of detailed codes to find the cause. You need both, used for different jobs.
analogy.breaks: Cars come with sensible warning lights from the factory. Databases don't, so you have to choose the SLIs and thresholds yourself and keep tuning them.

example.title: An SLO alert leads to one bad query
example.scenario: SLO: 99.9% of queries under 100 ms over 30 days. At 10:05 a burn-rate alert fires because the budget is being spent 14× faster than allowed.

steps.label: Is it real?
steps.detail: The dashboard shows p99 rising from 40 ms to 900 ms since the 09:50 deploy. Users are affected, so the page is justified.

steps.label: What's consuming time?
steps.detail: `pg_stat_statements` ordered by `total_exec_time` shows one new query shape at the top: 60% of all DB time.

steps.label: Why?
steps.detail: `EXPLAIN` shows a seq scan on `orders` filtered by `status`. The new feature filters on a column with no index.

steps.label: Mitigate, then fix
steps.detail: Turn the feature flag off (budget burn stops in minutes), then add the index `CONCURRENTLY` and turn the flag back on.

code.text:
-- Which query shapes cost the most overall?
SELECT left(query, 80) AS query, calls,
       round(total_exec_time)        AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS mean_ms
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 5;

-- Slow-burn check: how close is each database to transaction-ID wraparound?
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC;

example.outcome: alerted by user impact (not by CPU), pointed at the exact query shape within minutes, and mitigated by rolling back the change before attempting the real fix.

summary.core: Alert on what users feel (latency and errors against an SLO), then use query-level and saturation telemetry to find the cause. Watch slow-building risks as trends before they become incidents.
points: Page on **SLO burn**, not on CPU %.
`pg_stat_statements` is the single most useful Postgres diagnostic view. Turn it on everywhere.
Percentiles, not averages.
Disk, bloat and **XID age** are slow killers. Graph them and set capacity alerts days ahead.

check.q: Why is "CPU > 80%" a poor paging alert?
check.a: High CPU can be perfectly healthy (a busy but fast database) and low CPU can coexist with a lock-blocked outage. It doesn't measure user pain.

check.q: What does sorting pg_stat_statements by total_exec_time show that mean_exec_time doesn't?
check.a: Which queries consume the most database time overall. A 2 ms query called 10 M times often matters more than a 3 s query run once a day.
